newsitem.title: USA: U.S. bonds end sturdy, curve steepens on Greenspan.
newsitem.headline: U.S. bonds end sturdy, curve steepens on Greenspan.

text.p: Prices of U.S. Treasury securities ended higher after remarks by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan fueled active curve steepening trades and a big rally in two-, and five-year notes, analysts said.
The market pushed short-term interest rates lower, and also bought bonds, initially taking Greenspan's remarks as a hint the Fed may not need to tighten credit again when policymakers meet on May 20.
The benchmark 30-year bond closed up 16/32 at 96-19/32 to yield 6.90 percent.
Meanwhile, two-year notes rose 5/32 to 100-8/32 and five-year notes rose 11/32 to 100-14/32. Those yields ended at 6.24 percent and 6.52 percent, respectively.
"The bulk of the action overnight was in twos through fives, and a lot of buying in the front end of the market," said Roseanne Briggen, a treasury market analyst at MCM MoneyWatch.
Profit taking set in after the yield on the five-year note fell to about 6.5 percent and the spread between that security and the 30-year bond widened to 37 basis points, Briggen said.
"That is where all the steepening in the curve really came from -- fives-bonds," she said
A sharp slide in the dollar also helped curb the bond market's advance.

Treasuries then retreated from early highs, while the markets looked more closely and could not decide if the Fed chief was signaling an intention to hold rates steady this month or a warning of another hike in the federal funds rate.
"The central banker has accomplished his goals if people are totally befuddled afterwards," said Richard Hoey, chief economist at Dreyfus Corp.
"Given the fact you had opposite interpretations of what he said, Greenspan gave a very successful speech," said Hoey.

Greenspan told an audience in New York on Thursday night that he expected economic growth to slow later this year but added that the central bank would need to raise short-term interest rates if this does not become the case.

Trading volume was extremely heavy. At noon, the three- and five-year notes had posted their highest levels of activity since the beginning of 1996. But in absolute terms the two-year note had the highest volume, according to GovPX.
The three-year closed up 7/32 to yield 6.398 percent.
In early dealings, Asian central banks reportedly bought up to $2.0 billion in two-year notes.

"(Central banks) bought the front end of the Treasury market, despite the fact the dollar had dipped. I think they were making a bet on the currency, buying cheaper dollars to buy cheaper Treasuries," Briggen of MCM said.
In the U.S. session, the dollar continued to nosedive, sliding below 120 yen to its lowest level since late January and causing bonds to temporarily surrender their gains, analysts said.

"If you had the bond market now very worried about inflation risks, then the weak currency would have hurt it more," Hoey said. "But the bond market is relatively sanguine about the U.S. inflation risk."

San Francisco Fed chief Robert Parry struck a somewhat hawkish tone during the morning, saying the current level of resource utilization cannot persist with out becoming inflationary. But the remarks did little damage.
In bills, the three-month ended at 5.03 percent, down five basis points and the six-month bill was at 5.26 percent, off six basis points. (( -- 212-859-1667 ))
